title: What does React StrictMode do?
description: Development-only checks: double-invoked effects, double rendering, immutable-data warnings, and why StrictMode bugs are real bugs.

data.text: `<StrictMode>` is a **development-only** wrapper that activates extra checks and warnings to surface unsafe code. It double-invokes component bodies (render runs twice), runs effects mount → cleanup → mount again, and warns about: mutating state/props during render, outdated lifecycle usage, unsafe side effects in render, and legacy APIs. None of it ships in production builds — it costs nothing at runtime for users. Its signature feature is the **intentional effect double-invocation**, which simulates React 18's remounting behavior (e.g. reusing state on navigation) to expose effects that don't fully clean up. Code that breaks under StrictMode is genuinely buggy — it just happened to survive in a world without remounts.

**What it checks and how:**
- **Double rendering**: component function runs twice in dev — exposes side effects during render (fetch calls, subscriptions, mutations of module state). If render isn't pure, you'll see doubled log lines or doubled requests
- **Double-invoked effects**: dev lifecycle runs setup → cleanup → setup. Catches: missing cleanup (two subscriptions leak), non-idempotent setup (pushing to a module-level array twice), effects that assume they run once
- **Warnings**: mutating state directly (array.push on state), accessing context via old APIs, string refs, `findDOMNode`, legacy lifecycle methods, and impure renders
- **Pure-render enforcement**: if you mutate a prop or state object during render, StrictMode warns immediately

**The remounting model behind it:** React 18+ can discard and recreate state when you navigate away and back (e.g., in some router/framework scenarios). StrictMode's mount-unmount-mount in dev simulates this so you find bugs before production does.

**What it does NOT do:**
- Not a linter replacement — ESLint's react-hooks plugin catches rules-of-hooks and exhaustive-deps; StrictMode catches runtime impurity
- Not enabled in production builds — stripping it has zero user-facing effect; enabling it in prod *would* double-render and waste CPU
- Doesn't catch async mistakes — an uncancelled fetch still completes; it just runs setup twice so you might notice duplicated calls

**Practical advice:** keep `<StrictMode>` at the root forever. When an effect misbehaves only in dev, treat it as a gift: the cleanup is wrong. Common fixes: return cleanup that undoes everything, make setup idempotent, and never assume an effect runs exactly once.

data.title: What StrictMode exposes (and the fix)
A dev-only bug is still a bug
data.text: Effects that only run once today may run twice tomorrow — React's remounting behavior evolves, route transitions can remount subtrees, and Hot Module Replacement already remounts components. An effect that isn't cleanup-complete is a time bomb; StrictMode just detonates it early.

Interviewers want to assess:
- Knowing it's development-only and free in production
- The effect double-invocation pattern and what class of bug it reveals (missing cleanup)
- That double-render demands render purity
- Treating StrictMode warnings as actionable bug reports, not noise

items: Removing StrictMode because 'things run twice in dev' — the doubling is the point
Effects without cleanup that only manifest as doubled side effects
Doing side effects in the component body (fetch, subscribe) — double render means doubled work
Assuming StrictMode replaces linting — exhaustive-deps is ESLint's job
Expecting StrictMode to catch async races or unhandled rejections — it doesn't
Adding business logic that counts on exactly-one execution inside effects
Why can't React simply 'skip' the second effect run in dev?
How does effect double-invocation relate to route-change state restoration in React 18?
What other dev-only React features exist (Profiler, why-did-you-render)?
How do you write an idempotent effect?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: StrictMode: dev-only double rendering, effect double-invocation, impurity warnings
Its remount simulation exposes missing effect cleanup
Render must be pure; effects must be cleanup-complete
Zero production cost — keep it at the root always
data.takeaway: StrictMode is React running your component in the hardest possible dev conditions so that production's easier conditions never surprise you.
